subtopics.name: Main thread, Looper, and Handler fundamentals
Use cases and when to introduce them
Missing, unknown, nullable, and default JSON fields
Local vs remote sources of truth
What to share vs keep platform-specific

questions.text: Why should an Android app not rely on regular in-memory singletons to preserve user progress after the app is backgrounded?

answers.text: Because Android recreates every singleton on each Activity rotation even when the process remains alive.
Because the app process can be killed while backgrounded, clearing ordinary process memory.
Because singleton objects are stored in the manifest and cannot hold runtime data.
Because Kotlin object declarations are automatically persisted only on Android API 26 and lower.

questions.explanation: In-memory objects exist only inside the current app process. Android can kill a background process to reclaim resources, so user progress that must survive process death belongs in saved state or persistent storage.

questions.text: Which Android component is designed to expose a structured interface for sharing app-managed data with other apps?

answers.text: Activity
Service
ContentProvider
BroadcastReceiver

questions.explanation: A ContentProvider presents data through a standard provider interface. Activities own UI, services perform background work, and broadcast receivers react to broadcast events.

questions.text: A long-lived repository needs a Context only to access application resources. Which Context is safest to retain?

answers.text: The current Activity context, because it always updates after configuration changes.
The application context, because it is not tied to a specific Activity instance.
A View context, because Views outlive their Activity by default.
Any Context, because all Context implementations have the same lifecycle.

questions.explanation: A long-lived object should not retain an Activity context because that can leak the Activity. The application context is tied to the process and is appropriate for app-wide resource access.

questions.text: What is the main difference between an explicit Intent and an implicit Intent?

answers.text: An explicit Intent names a target component; an implicit Intent describes an action to resolve.
An explicit Intent can only start services; an implicit Intent can only start activities.
An explicit Intent crosses process boundaries; an implicit Intent never can.
An explicit Intent requires a PendingIntent; an implicit Intent cannot use one.

questions.explanation: An explicit Intent identifies the target component directly. An implicit Intent describes an action or data so the system can resolve a matching component.

questions.text: Why should expensive disk or network work not run directly on Android's main thread?

answers.text: Because the main thread cannot allocate memory.
Because only background threads can access Kotlin suspend functions.
Because blocking the main thread prevents timely UI rendering and input processing.
Because Android automatically kills any app that opens a file on the main thread.

questions.explanation: The main thread processes UI work and input events. Blocking it with expensive operations can freeze rendering and input handling, leading to jank or ANRs.

questions.text: What is the purpose of Android resource qualifiers such as layout-land or values-night?

answers.text: They make resources private to a single Activity.
They generate Kotlin constants for dependency injection.
They disable configuration changes for matching screens.
They provide alternative resources that Android selects for the current configuration.

questions.explanation: Resource qualifiers let Android select alternative resources for the current device configuration, such as orientation, locale, density, or night mode.

questions.text: Why is onPause() a poor place to perform a long database write or network request?

answers.text: Because onPause() is never called before another Activity starts.
Because onPause() should be brief and long work may not complete before the transition continues.
Because onPause() always runs on a background thread.
Because onPause() is called only after process death.

questions.explanation: onPause() execution is brief and should complete quickly. Longer shutdown or persistence work should use a more appropriate lifecycle point or background/persistence mechanism.

questions.text: In a Fragment that uses Views, why should view references normally be cleared in onDestroyView() rather than onDestroy()?

answers.text: Because the Fragment's View lifecycle can end before the Fragment instance is destroyed.
Because onDestroy() is never called for Fragments.
Because View references are valid until the process dies.
Because onDestroyView() runs only during configuration changes.

questions.explanation: A Fragment instance can outlive its View hierarchy. Clearing View references when the view is destroyed prevents retaining obsolete Views and their Activity context.

questions.text: What usually happens to an Activity during an unhandled configuration change such as rotation?

answers.text: The same Activity instance continues without lifecycle callbacks.
Only onResume() is called again.
The Activity is destroyed and a new instance is created.
The process is always killed before the Activity is recreated.

questions.explanation: By default, Android destroys and recreates the Activity for configuration changes. UI should be rebuilt from appropriate state rather than relying on old Activity fields.

questions.text: Why can a ViewModel preserve UI state across rotation but not by itself guarantee recovery after system-initiated process death?

answers.text: Because ViewModels are serialized into the manifest only during rotation.
Because ViewModels are scoped to a View and Views are never recreated.
Because process death preserves Activity fields but not ViewModels.
Because ViewModels are in-memory objects and process death clears that memory.

questions.explanation: ViewModels are retained in memory across configuration changes, but memory is lost when the process is killed. State that must recover after process death needs saved state or persistent storage.

questions.text: Which kind of state is a good candidate for saved-state APIs such as rememberSaveable or SavedStateHandle?

answers.text: Small transient UI state needed to restore the screen after recreation.
Large cached API responses that must be queried offline.
Open socket connections that should survive process death.
All repository data because saved state replaces local storage.

questions.explanation: Saved-state APIs are intended for small pieces of transient UI state needed to recreate the user's place. Large datasets or durable app data should use persistence.

questions.text: What does a navigation back stack primarily represent?

answers.text: A cache of every ViewModel created by the app.
An ordered history of navigation entries used to determine the current and previous destinations.
A list of all installed apps that can handle an Intent.
A set of resources selected for the current configuration.

questions.explanation: A back stack records destinations or entries in navigation order. Pushing a destination moves forward, and popping the top entry returns to the previous destination.

questions.text: In a typical single-stack navigation flow, what should happen when the user presses Back from a detail destination that was pushed from a list destination?

answers.text: Push a new copy of the list destination.
Restart the application process.
Pop the detail entry so the previous list entry becomes current again.
Clear every ViewModel in the application.

questions.explanation: Back should remove the current top entry and reveal the previous entry. It should not create a second copy of the list destination or clear unrelated application state.

questions.text: In the classic Android View system, what is the role of a ViewGroup?

answers.text: It stores app-wide singleton state for every screen.
It contains child Views and participates in measuring and laying them out.
It replaces the Activity lifecycle for UI code.
It is a resource qualifier for tablet layouts.

questions.explanation: A ViewGroup is a View that can contain child Views and is responsible for measuring and laying them out according to its layout rules.

questions.text: What is the high-level order of work in the classic Android View rendering pipeline?

answers.text: Measure, layout, then draw.
Draw, layout, then measure.
Inflate, serialize, then persist.
Compose, remember, then dispose.

questions.explanation: The View system first measures sizes, then lays out positions, then draws. Custom Views must respect this separation to render correctly.

questions.text: Why does RecyclerView rely on ViewHolder reuse for large lists?

answers.text: To make every list item share the same click listener identity.
To persist each row automatically across process death.
To prevent the adapter from ever receiving data changes.
To reduce repeated View inflation and allocation while scrolling.

questions.explanation: RecyclerView reuses item Views through ViewHolders so scrolling large datasets does not require inflating and allocating a new View hierarchy for every item that appears.

questions.text: Why should Compose UI be driven by observable state rather than directly mutating emitted UI nodes?

answers.text: Because Compose disables all mutable variables.
Because composables describe UI from state and are called again when observed state changes.
Because state objects are automatically written to Room.
Because recomposition happens only once per Activity lifetime.

questions.explanation: Compose is declarative. UI is described from current state, and state changes cause recomposition with new arguments instead of mutating previously emitted UI objects directly.

questions.text: What can cause a composable that reads Compose state to recompose?

answers.text: Only Activity recreation can cause recomposition.
Only explicit calls to invalidate() on a View can cause recomposition.
A change to observable state read by that composable.
Only a Gradle rebuild can cause recomposition.

questions.explanation: When a composable reads observable Compose state, changes to that state can invalidate the relevant composition and cause Compose to call the composable again with updated values.

questions.text: What is the usual goal of state hoisting in Compose?

answers.text: Move state to an appropriate owner and pass current value plus events down.
Store every UI value in a global singleton.
Prevent recomposition from ever happening.
Move state into XML resources so it can be localized.

questions.explanation: State hoisting moves state to an appropriate owner, often the lowest common ancestor that reads and writes it, which improves reuse, testability, and unidirectional data flow.

questions.text: Which statements about Compose side-effect APIs are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine scoped to the composition for its key set.
Side-effect APIs are required for every Text composable.
DisposableEffect can clean up resources when the effect leaves composition or keys change.
rememberCoroutineScope automatically runs its block during every recomposition.

questions.explanation: Side-effect APIs run work that should be coordinated with composition lifecycle. LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine tied to composition keys, and DisposableEffect provides cleanup when its keys change or it leaves composition.

questions.text: Why are stable item keys important in Compose lazy lists when items can be inserted, removed, or reordered?

answers.text: They make every row render on a background thread.
They replace the need for state hoisting.
They automatically persist list contents to disk.
They preserve item identity across insertions, removals, and moves.

questions.explanation: Stable keys let Compose keep item identity across dataset changes. That helps preserve item state and avoid treating moved items as unrelated new items.

questions.text: How can unstable parameter types affect Compose performance?

answers.text: They make the app fail to compile on Android only.
They can prevent Compose from skipping recomposition when inputs are effectively unchanged.
They force all state into SavedStateHandle.
They disable Material theming.

questions.explanation: If Compose cannot know whether a parameter's value has changed safely, it may recompose more often instead of skipping work. Stable immutable models can improve skippability.

questions.text: What is the purpose of semantics information in Compose?

answers.text: To choose which Gradle variant builds the composable.
To replace all content descriptions with bitmap snapshots.
To expose UI meaning and actions to accessibility services and testing APIs.
To make composables persist automatically after process death.

questions.explanation: Semantics describe UI meaning and actions to accessibility services and tests. They help non-visual users and automation understand the composable tree.

questions.text: What does Kotlin's type system express when a variable has nullable type String? instead of non-null type String?

answers.text: Both types can hold null; the difference is only documentation.
String is non-null, while String? is nullable.
String is nullable, while String? is non-null.
Nullability is checked only at runtime on Android.

questions.explanation: A non-null String type cannot hold null without unsafe interop or explicit tricks. Nullable types are written with a question mark, such as String?.

questions.text: What does a Kotlin data class primarily generate from properties declared in its primary constructor?

answers.text: Android Parcelable implementation for every property.
A Room table and DAO.
Value-oriented functions such as equals(), hashCode(), toString(), componentN(), and copy().
A sealed hierarchy and exhaustive when checks.

questions.explanation: Data classes generate value-oriented members such as equals(), hashCode(), toString(), componentN(), and copy() based on primary constructor properties.

questions.text: What is a Kotlin object declaration commonly used for?

answers.text: Declaring a singleton instance.
Declaring a class that must be instantiated with new.
Creating a nullable primitive type.
Generating a SQL table automatically.

questions.explanation: An object declaration defines a singleton instance. It is useful for stateless utilities or shared objects, but its in-memory state is still tied to the process.

questions.text: Why are sealed classes or sealed interfaces useful for modeling UI states or results?

answers.text: They allow any module to add new direct subclasses at runtime.
They make every subclass serializable without a plugin.
They prevent all inheritance inside the same package.
They model a restricted set of known alternatives.

questions.explanation: A sealed hierarchy restricts known direct subtypes, allowing callers to handle a closed set of cases and enabling exhaustive when expressions in many situations.

questions.text: In Kotlin generics, what does declaration-site variance with out T indicate?

answers.text: The type parameter can only be used as a function argument.
The type parameter is covariant and can be safely produced.
The type parameter disables null-safety checks.
The type parameter is erased only on Android.

questions.explanation: An out type parameter is covariant and can be produced safely by the type. It should not be consumed in positions that would break type safety.

questions.text: Why can an inline function with a reified type parameter check T at runtime?

answers.text: Because all Kotlin generic types are normally reified on the JVM.
Because reified type parameters are stored in Android resources.
Because the inline function body is expanded at call sites with the concrete type available.
Because reified works only for suspend functions.

questions.explanation: Inlining substitutes the function body at call sites, allowing the compiler to make the actual type argument available for operations such as is checks or class references.

questions.text: What is the difference between == and === in Kotlin?

answers.text: == checks structural equality; === checks referential equality.
== checks referential equality; === checks structural equality.
Both operators always compile to the same JVM instruction.
=== is only available for primitive numbers.

questions.explanation: The == operator checks structural equality by calling equals with null-safety. The === operator checks referential equality, meaning whether two references point to the same object.

questions.text: What is a practical risk of overusing Kotlin scope functions such as apply, also, let, run, and with?

answers.text: They disable null safety inside lambdas.
They make every lambda run on a background thread.
They turn immutable vals into mutable vars.
They can obscure receiver or argument meaning when nested or mixed heavily.

questions.explanation: Scope functions can reduce boilerplate, but excessive nesting or mixed receiver styles can make it unclear what this or it refers to and reduce readability.

questions.text: When can Kotlin sequences be useful compared with eager collection operations?

answers.text: When every element must be eagerly copied after each operation.
When a multi-step pipeline can benefit from lazy evaluation and fewer intermediate collections.
When code must run only on Android's main thread.
When nullability checks need to be disabled.

questions.explanation: Sequences evaluate operations lazily, which can avoid intermediate collections in multi-step pipelines. They are not automatically faster for every small collection.

questions.text: Why does JVM type erasure matter when designing generic Kotlin APIs for Android?

answers.text: Because erasure removes all objects from memory after compilation.
Because erasure makes nullable types impossible.
Because generic type arguments are generally not directly available at runtime.
Because erasure applies only to Compose previews.

questions.explanation: Generic type arguments are generally erased at runtime on the JVM, so APIs that need runtime type information often require an explicit class/token or an inline reified function.

questions.text: What does a suspend function indicate in Kotlin?

answers.text: It always runs on a new operating-system thread.
It can suspend without blocking the thread and resume later.
It is automatically retried after exceptions.
It can be called from any regular function with no coroutine context.

questions.explanation: A suspend function can suspend execution without blocking the underlying thread and later resume. It still needs to be called from another suspend function or coroutine.

questions.text: When is async more appropriate than launch?

answers.text: When the coroutine must ignore all cancellation.
When the coroutine should never have a parent Job.
When the caller needs a result represented by Deferred.
When the code must run synchronously on the caller thread.

questions.explanation: async returns a Deferred for a result that can be awaited. launch is better for fire-and-forget child work that does not directly produce a value.

questions.text: What problem does structured concurrency address?

answers.text: It keeps coroutine lifetimes tied to explicit scopes and parent-child relationships.
It guarantees every coroutine runs on Dispatchers.Main.
It disables exception propagation between child coroutines.
It converts every Flow into LiveData.

questions.explanation: Structured concurrency ties child coroutines to a parent scope so lifetimes, cancellation, and failure are managed predictably rather than leaving work running unowned.

questions.text: Why should long-running coroutine loops check for cancellation or call cancellable suspending functions?

answers.text: Because cancellation always interrupts the CPU instruction currently running.
Because cancelled coroutines are automatically restarted.
Because cancellation only works for network requests.
Because cancellation is cooperative and busy code must reach a cancellation check.

questions.explanation: Coroutine cancellation is cooperative. Code that never suspends and never checks cancellation may keep running even after its Job is cancelled.

questions.text: How does a regular Job parent usually react when one child coroutine fails with an uncaught exception?

answers.text: It ignores the failure and lets all children continue.
It is cancelled, and sibling children are cancelled as a consequence.
It retries the failed child automatically.
It converts the exception into null.

questions.explanation: In regular structured concurrency, an uncaught child failure cancels the parent, which then cancels its other children. Supervision changes that behavior.

questions.text: What is withContext commonly used for in Android coroutine code?

answers.text: Creating an unstructured global coroutine.
Launching two independent coroutines and returning immediately.
Switching execution context for a scoped block of suspending work.
Persisting coroutine state after process death.

questions.explanation: withContext runs a block in a different coroutine context, commonly switching blocking IO work to an IO dispatcher while preserving structured execution.

questions.text: What makes a basic Kotlin Flow cold?

answers.text: Its producer starts when the flow is collected.
It always stores the latest value in memory.
It emits only on Android's main thread.
It can have only one operator.

questions.explanation: A cold Flow does not run its producer until it is collected. Each collection can start the flow pipeline again.

questions.text: What does flowOn affect in a Kotlin Flow pipeline?

answers.text: Only the terminal collector block.
Every coroutine in the application process.
Only exception handlers attached to the Activity.
The upstream part of the flow before the flowOn operator.

questions.explanation: flowOn changes the context of upstream flow operations. It does not change the collector's coroutine context downstream.

questions.text: When is StateFlow a good fit for exposing UI state from a ViewModel?

answers.text: When each collector must receive a different one-time event.
When the UI needs the latest state value and updates when it changes.
When the state must be stored in SQLite automatically.
When there should be no initial value.

questions.explanation: StateFlow represents observable state with a current value. That matches screen UI state that Compose or other UI layers can observe.

questions.text: Which statements about SharedFlow are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It is a hot flow.
It must always have exactly one current value.
It is collected only once globally and then completes forever.
Its replay behavior is configurable.

questions.explanation: SharedFlow is a hot flow that can broadcast emissions to active collectors. Depending on replay configuration, it may or may not replay past values to new collectors.

questions.text: Why is separation of concerns important in Android architecture?

answers.text: It guarantees that every screen needs only one class.
It removes the need for tests.
It keeps responsibilities focused so changes and tests affect smaller parts of the app.
It requires all code to live in the data layer.

questions.explanation: Separating UI, state, data access, and business rules reduces coupling and makes each part easier to test, replace, and reason about.

questions.text: In unidirectional data flow, how do state and events usually move?

answers.text: State flows down to consumers, and events flow up to the state owner.
Events and state both mutate every UI element directly.
Only repositories are allowed to observe state.
State must always be stored in global mutable objects.

questions.explanation: State flows from the owner toward the UI, and events flow back toward the owner that can decide how state changes.

questions.text: What role does a repository usually play in Android app architecture?

answers.text: It renders composables directly.
It coordinates access to one or more data sources behind a focused API.
It replaces the Activity lifecycle.
It must contain all navigation routes.

questions.explanation: A repository mediates app data operations and can coordinate local and remote data sources while exposing data to higher layers through a stable API.

questions.text: What does single source of truth mean for a piece of application data?

answers.text: Every screen keeps its own independent mutable copy.
The network is always the source of truth, even offline.
Only XML resources can hold the data.
One owner is responsible for the data and exposes it to consumers.

questions.explanation: A single owner is responsible for changing and exposing that data. This avoids conflicting copies and makes updates traceable.

questions.text: Why should UI state have a clear owner?

answers.text: So state changes have one responsible place and can be exposed predictably.
So every child composable can mutate the same backing field.
So state can avoid lifecycle concerns entirely.
So state never needs to be tested.

questions.explanation: A clear owner controls mutation and exposes observable state, reducing accidental conflicting updates from multiple parts of the UI.

questions.text: What problem does dependency inversion help solve between domain logic and data implementations?

answers.text: It forces domain code to import every database class.
It removes all runtime dependencies from the app.
It keeps higher-level logic from depending directly on concrete implementation details.
It makes networking run faster by default.

questions.explanation: Dependency inversion lets higher-level policy depend on abstractions instead of concrete lower-level details, making implementations replaceable and tests easier.

questions.text: When is adding a use-case layer most defensible in an Android feature?

answers.text: Always, even when it only forwards one repository call unchanged.
When it contains meaningful business rules or orchestration that would otherwise be duplicated or misplaced.
Only when the UI is XML instead of Compose.
Never, because repositories must contain all business rules.

questions.explanation: A use-case layer earns its place when it centralizes meaningful reusable business rules or coordinates multiple dependencies. Adding one for trivial pass-through calls can create needless indirection.

questions.text: Why is constructor injection often preferred for required dependencies?

answers.text: It makes required dependencies explicit at construction time.
It hides dependencies behind global mutable state.
It requires Android reflection for every object.
It prevents unit testing without instrumentation.

questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, allows immutable properties, and lets tests construct the class directly with fakes.

questions.text: What is the role of a composition root in manual dependency injection?

answers.text: It stores UI state for every composable.
It validates JSON schemas at runtime.
It centralizes construction and wiring of application dependencies.
It replaces stable IDs in content models.

questions.explanation: The composition root is where object graphs are assembled. Keeping wiring there avoids hidden lookups spread through feature code.

questions.text: Which statements about DI scopes are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: A scope always means the object lives forever.
A scope controls the lifetime and sharing boundary of provided instances.
A shorter-lived object can safely be retained by any longer-lived singleton without risk.
Incorrect scoping can create leaks or unintended shared state.

questions.explanation: A scope defines how long a provided instance is shared. Mis-scoping can cause unnecessary recreation or leaks when a long-lived object holds a short-lived dependency.

questions.text: What is a common downside of a service locator compared with explicit dependency injection?

answers.text: It makes all dependencies visible in constructors.
It can hide dependencies and lifecycle assumptions behind runtime lookup.
It prevents any object from being shared.
It is required by Kotlin Multiplatform.

questions.explanation: A service locator hides dependency lookup inside implementation code, making dependencies less visible and often making tests and lifecycle boundaries harder to reason about.

questions.text: Which storage option is usually appropriate for small key-value user preferences that must survive process death?

answers.text: An Activity field.
DataStore.
A RecyclerView adapter.
A Compose remember block only.

questions.explanation: DataStore is a modern Jetpack option for small preference or typed data. Large relational datasets are a better fit for a database such as Room.

questions.text: What is the responsibility of a Room DAO?

answers.text: Rendering database rows in Compose.
Declaring notification channels.
Defining database queries and access methods.
Choosing Gradle build variants.

questions.explanation: A DAO defines database access methods and queries for Room. Entities model tables; repositories decide how database data is used by the app.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: Why are database transactions important when multiple related writes must succeed or fail together?

answers.text: They provide atomicity for related operations.
They force every query onto the main thread.
They replace schema migrations.
They automatically sync data to the network.

questions.explanation: A transaction groups related operations atomically. If one part fails, the database can avoid committing a partially updated state.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: What is useful about returning Flow from a Room query?

answers.text: It makes the query run without a database.
It guarantees network freshness.
It disables transactions for the DAO.
It lets collectors receive updated query results as data changes.

questions.explanation: Observable Room queries can emit updates when table data changes, letting UI observe local data and update from the database source of truth.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: In an offline-first app, why is a local data source commonly treated as the source of truth?

answers.text: Because offline-first apps should never contact a server.
Because the app can remain usable and consistent when the network is unavailable.
Because local data is always more recent than remote data.
Because Android forbids caching network responses.

questions.explanation: The UI can read usable data without waiting for the network, while synchronization updates the local source when connectivity allows.

questions.text: Why does HTTP idempotency matter when designing retry behavior?

answers.text: It means the request never reaches the server.
It means every method is safe to retry forever.
It helps determine whether retrying a request may repeat unintended side effects.
It applies only to WebSocket messages.

questions.explanation: Idempotent operations can be repeated with the same intended effect, making retries safer. Retrying non-idempotent operations such as many POST requests can duplicate side effects unless designed carefully.

questions.text: Why should Android network clients configure timeouts?

answers.text: To make TLS optional.
To bound waiting time for network operations that may stall.
To force every response into the disk cache.
To make all HTTP methods idempotent.

questions.explanation: Timeouts bound how long the app waits for connection, reading, or writing. Without them, calls can hang too long and degrade user experience or resource usage.

questions.text: What is a common use of an OkHttp interceptor?

answers.text: Adding headers or observing/modifying requests and responses.
Declaring Room entities.
Rendering Compose layouts.
Replacing Gradle dependency resolution.

questions.explanation: Interceptors can observe, modify, and retry requests/responses. Common uses include adding headers, logging, and handling authentication concerns.

questions.text: What is the benefit of declaring Retrofit service functions as suspend functions?

answers.text: They make HTTP responses impossible to fail.
They force the call to run on the main thread.
They remove the need to parse response bodies.
They integrate asynchronous calls with coroutine suspension.

questions.explanation: Suspend service functions integrate network calls into coroutine code without blocking the calling thread, letting callers use structured coroutine handling.

questions.text: What is a key difference between kotlinx.serialization and reflection-heavy JSON libraries?

answers.text: It works only on Android and cannot be used in common code.
It uses compiler-assisted serializers and supports Kotlin Multiplatform.
It requires every model to be a Room entity.
It serializes only XML resources.

questions.explanation: kotlinx.serialization uses compiler-generated serializers for annotated models and is designed for Kotlin multiplatform use, rather than depending primarily on runtime reflection.

questions.text: A deferrable sync should survive process death and run only when network connectivity is available. Which API is the best fit?

answers.text: A raw Thread stored in a singleton.
A ViewModel coroutine.
WorkManager with a network constraint.
A composable side effect with no persistence.

questions.explanation: WorkManager is intended for deferrable persistent work and supports constraints such as required network connectivity.

questions.text: When is a foreground service generally appropriate?

answers.text: For user-noticeable ongoing work that must continue and be visible to the user.
For any short database query from a ViewModel.
For replacing every WorkManager task.
For hiding background work from system restrictions.

questions.explanation: Foreground services are for user-noticeable work that must continue while the app is not in the foreground and must show an ongoing notification.

questions.text: For apps targeting modern Android versions, why do foreground service types matter?

answers.text: They choose the app's launcher icon.
They declare the foreground work category and related requirements.
They make a service run without a notification.
They replace runtime permissions.

questions.explanation: Foreground service types declare the category of foreground work and can carry type-specific permissions and runtime prerequisites.

questions.text: Why should Android apps choose background APIs with OS limits in mind?

answers.text: Because background restrictions apply only to debug builds.
Because every background task gets unlimited CPU time.
Because WorkManager cannot use constraints.
Because the OS restricts background execution to protect battery and system health.

questions.explanation: Android applies background execution and battery restrictions. Choosing the wrong API can make work unreliable, blocked, or wasteful.

questions.text: Why do Android notification channels matter?

answers.text: They replace PendingIntent for notification taps.
They are required only for FCM data messages.
They give users category-level control over notification behavior.
They store notification history in Room.

questions.explanation: Notification channels group notifications into user-controllable categories. On supported Android versions, channel importance and settings affect how notifications appear.

questions.text: For Android 13 and higher, what must most apps do before posting non-exempt notifications?

answers.text: Declare only INTERNET permission.
Request the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission.
Start a bound service.
Create a Room migration.

questions.explanation: Android 13 introduced the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission for most non-exempt notifications. Apps should request it at an appropriate time.

questions.text: What is a practical difference between FCM notification messages and data messages?

answers.text: Data messages carry custom payloads for app handling; notification messages can be displayed by the SDK depending on app state.
Data messages never reach Android devices.
Notification messages require Room.
Both message types are always handled identically in every app state.

questions.explanation: Notification messages can be handled/displayed by the SDK depending on app state, while data messages deliver custom key-value payloads for app code to handle.

questions.text: Why should Android test strategy include more than only end-to-end UI tests?

answers.text: Because UI tests cannot interact with Android views.
Because focused lower-level tests are faster and isolate failures more precisely.
Because unit tests replace all integration tests.
Because Compose code cannot be tested.

questions.explanation: Lower-level tests are usually faster, more focused, and better at isolating failures. UI tests are valuable but slower and more brittle when used as the only safety net.

questions.text: What is a common reason to use a fake implementation in a unit test?

answers.text: To make the test depend on the production server.
To hide all assertions.
To replace a dependency with deterministic behavior under test.
To force every test to be instrumented.

questions.explanation: A fake can provide deterministic behavior for a dependency while preserving a realistic contract, making the class under test easier to exercise.

questions.text: Why are ViewModels often good candidates for local unit tests?

answers.text: Their state transitions can often be tested without rendering UI.
They require a physical device for every assertion.
They cannot accept fake dependencies.
They are recreated after every function call.

questions.explanation: ViewModels can expose state and handle events without depending directly on rendering. With dependencies injected, their state transitions can be tested locally.

questions.text: What is the purpose of runTest in coroutine tests?

answers.text: To run tests only on Android devices.
To disable coroutine cancellation.
To make all delays sleep the real thread.
To test suspending code with a controlled coroutine test environment.

questions.explanation: runTest provides a coroutine test scope and scheduler support so suspending code can be tested deterministically, including virtual-time behavior.

questions.text: Why do Compose UI tests often query by semantics rather than implementation details?

answers.text: Because semantics are private compiler metadata.
Because semantics expose meaningful UI information for testing and accessibility.
Because semantics replace all assertions.
Because Compose tests cannot click buttons.

questions.explanation: Semantics represent user-visible meaning and actions. Querying semantics makes tests align better with accessibility and behavior than with internal layout structure.

questions.text: What is a common cause of an ANR in an Android app?

answers.text: Using immutable data classes.
Collecting a StateFlow from Compose.
Blocking the main thread with long-running work.
Using a version catalog.

questions.explanation: ANRs occur when the app does not respond to input or lifecycle-related work in time. Blocking the main thread with expensive work is a common cause.

questions.text: How can retaining an Activity reference in a singleton cause a memory leak?

answers.text: The singleton can keep the Activity reachable after its lifecycle should end.
The Activity becomes stored in Android resources.
The garbage collector never runs in Android apps.
The Activity is converted into a Service.

questions.explanation: A singleton can outlive an Activity instance. If it strongly references the Activity, the old Activity and its Views may remain reachable after they should be collected.

questions.text: What is a reasonable way to reduce unnecessary recomposition work in Compose?

answers.text: Store all UI state in global mutable variables.
Avoid using state anywhere in the UI.
Make every parameter nullable.
Use stable immutable models and keep state changes scoped to where they are needed.

questions.explanation: Stable immutable parameters and careful state ownership help Compose skip work when inputs have not changed. The goal is not to prevent recomposition entirely.

questions.text: Why should expensive initialization be treated carefully during app startup?

answers.text: Because startup code cannot allocate objects.
Because synchronous startup work can delay first draw and user interaction.
Because startup work always runs after the app is closed.
Because Android requires every dependency to be initialized in Application.onCreate().

questions.explanation: Too much synchronous startup work delays first draw and can hurt launch performance. Non-critical work should be deferred or made lazy where appropriate.

questions.text: Why should an app request a runtime permission close to the user action that needs it?

answers.text: Because permissions requested at startup are always ignored by Android.
Because runtime permissions are granted automatically when requested later.
Because contextual requests explain the purpose and improve user trust.
Because permissions are stored only in a ViewModel.

questions.explanation: Requesting permission in context helps users understand why access is needed and supports a better permission UX than requesting everything at startup.

questions.text: Why should exported Android components be reviewed carefully?

answers.text: Because other apps may be able to invoke them.
Because exported components cannot receive Intents.
Because exported components are always private to the app.
Because exporting a component disables all permissions.

questions.explanation: Exported components can be invoked by other apps. They need intentional permissions, input validation, and minimal exposure.

questions.text: Why should access tokens, personal data, and secrets be excluded from logs?

answers.text: Because logs cannot contain strings.
Because Android automatically encrypts every log line.
Because logging secrets improves crash triage safely.
Because logs can expose sensitive data beyond the intended security boundary.

questions.explanation: Logs can be retained, shared, or accessed during debugging and support. Sensitive data in logs increases privacy and account-compromise risk.

questions.text: Why does Gradle distinguish dependency configurations such as implementation, api, and runtimeOnly?

answers.text: To choose the Android launcher icon.
To model how dependencies are declared, resolved, and exposed.
To replace source sets with XML resources.
To make every dependency global to all modules.

questions.explanation: Configurations define the role and scope of dependencies, such as compile classpath exposure, runtime-only use, or publication to consumers.

questions.text: What problem do Gradle version catalogs solve in a multi-module project?

answers.text: They compile Kotlin source files.
They replace dependency resolution with manual downloads.
They centralize dependency coordinates and versions behind reusable aliases.
They store runtime user preferences.

questions.explanation: Version catalogs centralize dependency and plugin coordinates so modules can use consistent aliases rather than duplicating literal versions.

questions.text: What is a key difference between an APK and an Android App Bundle?

answers.text: An APK is installable; an App Bundle is a publishing format used to generate optimized APKs.
An App Bundle is the only format that can run on an emulator directly.
An APK contains only source code and no resources.
They are identical files with different extensions.

questions.explanation: An APK is directly installable on a device. An Android App Bundle is a publishing format that lets Google Play generate optimized APKs for devices.

questions.text: A news app must remain readable during poor connectivity. Which design choice best supports that requirement?

answers.text: Block the UI until every network request succeeds.
Read from a local source of truth and sync remote updates in the background.
Store all state only in Activity fields.
Disable caching to avoid stale data.

questions.explanation: An offline-first design reads from a local source of truth and synchronizes with the network when possible, keeping the UI useful during connectivity problems.

questions.text: When designing background sync for mobile, which constraints should be considered? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Network availability and metering.
Battery and charging state.
Whether the feature uses a specific button color.
OS background execution limits and retry policy.

questions.explanation: Mobile sync design must account for network availability, battery, OS background limits, and retry behavior. Ignoring those constraints produces unreliable or wasteful sync.

questions.text: What is a good rule of thumb when deciding what to put in Kotlin Multiplatform common code?

answers.text: Put every line of code in commonMain, even platform API calls.
Avoid common code entirely in KMP projects.
Share platform-independent logic and use platform source sets for platform APIs.
Use expect/actual for every class by default.

questions.explanation: Common code should hold behavior that is genuinely platform-independent or expressed through a useful common contract. Platform-specific UI or APIs should stay in platform source sets unless there is a good abstraction.

questions.text: What problem do expect and actual declarations solve in Kotlin Multiplatform?

answers.text: They let common code depend on a common declaration with platform-specific implementations.
They automatically convert Android Views into SwiftUI.
They replace Gradle source sets.
They serialize content models without annotations.

questions.explanation: An expect declaration defines a common API, and each platform supplies the actual implementation. This is useful when shared code needs a platform-specific capability behind a common contract.
